opening: Brazil votes in a presidential runoff that could shift Latin America’s largest country sharply right, France is counting the cost of another mass protest day, and a U.S. intelligence warning says Iranian-linked plots against Americans have advanced as the Gulf conflict continues.

stories.threadSummary: Brazil’s presidential campaign and runoff between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro.
stories.title: Brazil votes in knife-edge runoff between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro
stories.body: Brazilians began voting Sunday in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro after Bolsonaro unexpectedly led the first round 47% to 45%. Final polling showed the race effectively tied. The result could either give Lula an unprecedented fourth non-consecutive term or move Latin America’s largest country toward a government closely aligned with U.S. President Donald Trump.
stories.whatChanged: The close campaign moved from its final rallies into voting, with the presidency and Brazil’s foreign-policy direction now being decided.
stories.whyMatters: Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and most populous country. A Bolsonaro victory would reinforce the region’s recent rightward electoral shift and likely tighten relations with Washington; a Lula victory would preserve a major counterweight to that trend.
stories.uncertainty: Voting had only begun by the evidence cutoff. Final polls were close enough that neither candidate had a clear advantage, and no result was available.
stories.watchNext: Turnout, the speed and margin of the electronic count, whether either side contests the result, and the composition of the governing coalition the winner can assemble in a more conservative Congress.
keyFacts: Flavio Bolsonaro led the first round with 47% to Lula’s 45%
Final polling showed the runoff effectively tied
Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive presidential term
Bolsonaro has promised closer ties with Washington and a pardon for his father

report.heading: A presidency decided after an upset
paragraphs: Brazil opened polling stations Sunday after a campaign transformed by Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round upset. The senator, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished two points ahead of Lula despite polls that had not anticipated his lead. Lula narrowed the gap during the runoff campaign, leaving the final surveys effectively tied.

The campaign has centered on living costs, corruption, crime and Brazil’s relationship with the United States. Lula has accused Washington of political interference, which the United States denies, while Bolsonaro has presented Donald Trump as an ally and promised a tougher approach to crime.

report.heading: A regional choice as well as a domestic one
paragraphs: The result will shape more than Brazil’s domestic policy. A Bolsonaro victory would add Latin America’s largest country to a broader run of right-leaning governments friendly to Trump. Lula, by contrast, has maintained a more independent foreign policy and clashed with Washington over trade and security.

Congress also shifted right in the first round, meaning either president would govern in a different legislative environment. The immediate uncertainty is electoral rather than interpretive: Brazil’s electronic count is fast, but no result existed at the morning cutoff and the closeness of the race makes the margin important as well as the winner.

stories.threadSummary: Protests, riots and the French government's response during the 2026 political and cost-of-living crisis.
stories.title: France counts 410,000 protesters as violence returns after mostly peaceful marches
stories.body: France’s Interior Ministry counted about 410,000 people in nationwide demonstrations Saturday, while unions put participation at roughly twice that level. Most marches were peaceful, but violence and looting flared in Paris, Marseille and several other cities after dark. Police used tear gas and water cannon after the government deployed 70,000 officers and gendarmes for the day.
stories.whatChanged: The security operation described in Saturday morning’s edition now has an outcome: mass turnout, largely peaceful daytime marches and renewed pockets of violence after dark.
stories.whyMatters: The protests remain large enough to sustain pressure on the government over living costs and public services, while recurring violence gives authorities a rationale for tighter controls that could itself deepen political anger.
stories.uncertainty: The Interior Ministry and unions gave sharply different turnout estimates, and the full totals for arrests, injuries and damage were still developing after the demonstrations.
stories.watchNext: Whether unions call another national protest, the final arrest and injury figures, and whether the government changes economic policy or further tightens protest restrictions.
keyFacts: The Interior Ministry estimated 410,000 protesters nationwide
Unions claimed roughly twice the official turnout
Violence flared in Paris, Marseille and other cities after mostly peaceful marches

report.heading: The feared protest day arrives
paragraphs: Hundreds of thousands marched across France on Saturday against rising living costs, inequality and government economic policy. The Interior Ministry estimated 410,000 participants nationwide; unions said the number was about twice as high. The gap is typical of French protest counting but leaves the precise scale disputed.

Most demonstrations remained peaceful through the day. As evening approached, however, violent groups clashed with police in Paris, Marseille and other cities, and some shops were looted. Police used tear gas and water cannon. The government had deployed 70,000 officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than the previous weekend.

report.heading: A political problem that policing cannot settle
paragraphs: The demonstrations are rooted in complaints about purchasing power, inequality and strained public services. Authorities distinguish those protesters from groups they accuse of seeking confrontation or theft, but the two dynamics increasingly overlap in the public debate over how the government should respond.

Saturday therefore produced a mixed result: the security deployment prevented the day from becoming uniformly violent, but it did not end the unrest or prevent serious clashes. Whether the movement persists now depends on both the organizers’ next steps and the government’s response to the underlying economic grievances.

stories.threadTitle: The Iran war and Gulf security
stories.threadSummary: The widening conflict around Iran and its effects on Gulf states, shipping and energy infrastructure.
stories.title: U.S. intelligence warns Iranian-linked plots against Americans have advanced
stories.body: A U.S. intelligence memo dated October 23 warned that Iran had intensified efforts to target American personnel and that lethal plots against U.S. citizens had reached advanced stages in the Middle East and elsewhere, Reuters reported. The warning comes as Washington reduces diplomatic staffing in Saudi Arabia and updates travel advice across the region amid renewed Houthi attacks and continuing pressure around the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.whatChanged: The conflict’s risk picture widened beyond missiles, shipping and infrastructure to an explicit U.S. intelligence warning about advanced plots against individual Americans.
stories.whyMatters: Credible plots against U.S. personnel could drive further embassy drawdowns, travel restrictions or retaliation and make de-escalation harder even while Iranian officials publicly argue for renewed negotiations.
stories.uncertainty: The memo does not publicly identify targets, locations or operational details, and the underlying intelligence cannot be independently assessed from the reporting.
stories.watchNext: Additional U.S. security measures, any arrests or disrupted plots, further Houthi attacks, and whether renewed Iranian calls for negotiations produce a concrete diplomatic channel.
keyFacts: The warning was contained in an October 23 U.S. intelligence memo
It said some lethal plots had reached advanced stages
The United States has reduced non-emergency diplomatic staffing in Saudi Arabia
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian has separately called for another attempt at an interim deal

report.heading: A different kind of escalation warning
paragraphs: Reuters reported that an October 23 memo from the U.S. director of national intelligence warned Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Iranian efforts to target American personnel had increased and that some lethal plots were at advanced stages. The warning covered threats in the Middle East and other countries but did not publicly identify specific targets or operational details.

The assessment comes amid broader security precautions. Washington has reduced staffing at its diplomatic mission in Saudi Arabia and updated travel advisories for a number of countries as Houthi attacks and Iranian-linked threats complicate security across the Gulf.

report.heading: Security pressure alongside diplomacy
paragraphs: The intelligence warning arrives at the same time as Iranian leaders continue to signal interest in renewed negotiations. President Massoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that another attempt should be made at an interim agreement, while Tehran’s ambassador in Pakistan said Iran remained open to talks under a Pakistan-brokered framework.

Those tracks can coexist: governments often negotiate while preparing for escalation. But advanced plots against U.S. citizens, if confirmed or disrupted, would raise the political cost of diplomacy and could trigger retaliation. The public reporting establishes the warning, not the operational details behind it.

stories.threadSummary: Protests across Europe over living costs, public services and government economic policy.
stories.title: Belgian police and protesters clash during education demonstrations
stories.body: Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray during clashes with mostly young demonstrators in Brussels demanding better education funding and protesting police violence. Police detained five people for disturbing public order and arrested four others over prohibited weapons and alleged incitement to riot. The clashes were smaller than Belgium’s previous week of demonstrations and the much larger protests in neighboring France.
stories.whatChanged: A broader European protest wave produced another confrontation in Brussels, though on a smaller scale than the unrest in France.

stories.threadSummary: How AI investment, adoption and automation are changing work, productivity and economic power.
stories.title: IMF and OECD warn AI could widen the divide between rich and poor countries
stories.hook: The institutions now framing AI as a growth engine are also warning that electricity, compute and skills could determine which countries capture the gains.
stories.body: The IMF and OECD warned that artificial intelligence could widen gaps between richer and poorer countries unless access to electricity, digital infrastructure and skills improves. The IMF estimates effective AI adoption could add as much as 0.5 percentage point to annual global growth over the medium term, but both institutions say actual productivity gains remain limited and adoption is uneven.
stories.whatChanged: Two major international economic institutions put distributional risk alongside growth in their assessment of the AI investment boom.
stories.whyMatters: If AI productivity gains depend heavily on power, compute, capital and skilled workers, countries already strong in those inputs may compound their advantage rather than technology diffusing benefits evenly.
stories.uncertainty: The productivity estimates are scenarios rather than measured gains; workplace adoption and returns on the current infrastructure buildout remain uncertain.
stories.watchNext: Evidence of measured productivity gains, infrastructure investment outside wealthy economies, and policies aimed at skills and access rather than only model development.
keyFacts: The IMF says effective AI adoption could add up to 0.5 percentage point to annual global growth over the medium term
The OECD estimates AI could add 0.4 to 1.2 percentage points to annual productivity growth in member countries
The IMF estimates about 40% of jobs worldwide could be exposed to AI
Both institutions warn infrastructure and skills gaps could widen inequality between countries

report.heading: Growth with a distribution problem
paragraphs: The IMF and OECD are increasingly treating artificial intelligence as a macroeconomic variable rather than only a technology-sector story. Their latest assessments point to potentially meaningful productivity gains but stress that the gains depend on adoption, infrastructure and complementary skills.

Those prerequisites are unevenly distributed. Wealthier countries and firms can finance data centres, electricity supply, advanced chips and training more readily, creating a mechanism through which the AI boom could widen existing economic gaps even if global output rises.

report.heading: Forecasts are not yet outcomes
paragraphs: The headline growth estimates remain conditional. The IMF says effective adoption could lift annual global growth by as much as half a percentage point over the medium term, while the OECD estimates a 0.4-to-1.2-point productivity boost across its members. Neither figure is a measured present-day effect.

That distinction matters because infrastructure spending has raced ahead of demonstrated economy-wide productivity gains. The useful signal is therefore not that AI has already produced the forecast growth, but that major economic institutions are now focusing on who has the capacity to convert model capability into durable productivity.
